content: Infectious mononucleosis (IM), commonly caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), is a clinical syndrome characterized by symptoms such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and sore throat. It predominantly affects older teenagers and young adults. While IM is generally a self-limiting and benign illness requiring only symptomatic management, some cases may have a prolonged or complicated course, potentially impacting productivity in school or work settings. Antiviral medications have been explored as a treatment option for IM, aiming to inhibit viral replication and suppress viral activity. However, the use of antivirals in IM remains controversial, and no established guidelines currently exist for their use in this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of antiviral therapy in the management of IM. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, and Web of Science, up to April 2016. Additionally, clinical trial registries were searched for completed and ongoing studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing antiviral therapy with placebo or no treatment in immunocompetent individuals of any age or sex who had a clinical and laboratory-confirmed diagnosis of IM with symptoms lasting up to 14 days. Seven RCTs involving a total of 333 participants were included in the review. The studies varied in terms of setting (hospitalized versus outpatient), participant age (ranging from two years to young adults), type of antiviral used (acyclovir, valomaciclovir, and valacyclovir), route of administration, and treatment duration. Follow-up periods ranged from 20 days to six months. The diagnosis of IM in these studies was based on clinical symptoms and laboratory findings. The risk of bias in all included studies was assessed as either unclear or high, and the quality of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low. The review found statistically significant improvements in two of the 12 outcomes assessed, but these improvements were of questionable clinical relevance. For example, there was a mean reduction in the time to clinical recovery (as assessed by a physician) of five days in the treatment group compared to the control group. However, the confidence intervals were wide (95% CI -8.04 to -1.08), and the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain, especially given that symptoms of IM can persist for a month or longer, with fatigue lasting up to six months in approximately 10% of patients. Adverse events and side effects of antiviral medications were reported narratively in five studies. In some cases, it was unclear whether adverse events were related to the medication or the disease itself. Overall, most studies did not find significant differences in adverse events between the treatment and control groups. Due to the potential for double counting, these results could not be pooled. A mean reduction in the duration of lymphadenopathy by nine days (95% CI -11.75 to -6.14) was observed in the treatment group compared to the control group. Regarding viral shedding, antiviral therapy was found to suppress viral shedding during treatment, but this effect was not sustained after the treatment was discontinued. For all other outcomes, including complications, health-related quality of life, days missed from school or work, and economic outcomes, no statistically significant differences were observed between the antiviral and control groups. In conclusion, the effectiveness of antiviral agents such as acyclovir, valomaciclovir, and valacyclovir in the treatment of acute IM remains uncertain. The evidence supporting their use is of very low quality, and the majority of included studies were at high or unclear risk of bias. While two outcomes showed results favoring antiviral treatment, the clinical significance of these findings is questionable. Decision-makers should weigh the lack of robust evidence for effectiveness against potential adverse events, costs, and the risk of antiviral resistance. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the role of antiviral therapy in the management of IM.
